etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English engyn, from Anglo-Norman engine, Old French engin (“skill, cleverness, war machine”), from Latin ingenium (“innate or natural quality, nature, genius, a genius, an invention, (in Late Latin) a war-engine, battering-ram”), related to ingignō (“to instil by birth, implant, produce in”). Compare gin, ingenious, engineer.

definitions.definition: A large construction used in warfare, such as a battering ram, catapult etc. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: c. 1587–1588, [Christopher Marlowe], Tamburlaine the Great.  […]  The First Part […], 2nd edition, part 1, London:  […]  [R. Robinson for] Richard Iones, […], published 1592, →OCLC; reprinted as Tamburlaine the Great (A Scolar Press Facsimile), Menston, Yorkshire, London: Scolar Press, 1973, →ISBN, Act IIII, scene i:
quote.text: Their warlike Engins and munitionExceed the forces of their martial men.

definitions.definition: (now archaic) A tool; a utensil or implement. [from 14th c.]

quote.citation: 1714, Bernard Mandeville, The Fable of the Bees:
quote.text: Flattery must be the most powerful Argument that cou'd be used to Human Creatures. Making use of this bewitching Engine, they extoll'd the Excellency of our Nature above other Animals [...].

quote.citation: 1733, [Alexander Pope], An Essay on Man. […], epistle I, London: Printed for J[ohn] Wilford, […], →OCLC, page 15, lines 248–251:
quote.text: What if the Foot, ordain'd the duſt to tread, / Or Hand, to toil, aſpir'd to be the Head? / What if the Head, the Eye, or Ear repin'd / To ſerve mere Engines to the ruling Mind?

definitions.definition: A complex mechanical device which converts energy into useful motion or physical effects. [from 16th c.]
A person or group of people which influence a larger group; a driving force. [from 16th c.]

quote.citation: 1834, L[etitia] E[lizabeth] L[andon], chapter VII, in Francesca Carrara. […], volume I, London: Richard Bentley, […], (successor to Henry Colburn), →OCLC, page 75:
quote.text: In France, the parliament soon became a mere engine in the hands of a few high-born and ambitious men, who had nothing in common with its interests, which were those of the people.

definitions.definition: The part of a car or other vehicle which provides the force for motion, now especially one powered by internal combustion. [from 19th c.]
A self-powered vehicle, especially a locomotive, used for pulling cars along a track. [from 19th c.]
(computing) A software or hardware system responsible for a specific technical task (usually with qualifying word). [from 20th c.]
(obsolete) The result of cunning; something ingenious, a contrivance; (in negative senses) a plot, a scheme. [13th–18th c.]

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto I”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, page 193:
quote.text: Therefore this craftie engine he did frame, / Againſt his praiſe to ſtirre vp enmitye [...].

definitions.definition: Anything used to effect a purpose; any device or contrivance; an agent.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene v], page 243, column 1:
quote.text: [...] their promiſes, entiſements, oathes, tokens, and all theſe engines of luſt [...].

quote.citation: 1678, John Bunyan, “The Author’s Apology for His Book”, in The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That which is to Come: […], London:  […]  Nath[aniel] Ponder […], →OCLC:
quote.text: You ſee the ways the Fiſher-man doth take / To catch the Fiſh; what Engins doth he make?

definitions.definition: (transitive, dated) To equip with an engine; said especially of steam vessels.
(transitive, obsolete) To assault with an engine.

quote.text: to engine and batter our walls

definitions.definition: (transitive, obsolete) To contrive; to put into action.
